Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (£62bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.
A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the loss-making business meant more stock was sold than originally planned. Anthropic's shares have been priced at $83, up from the proposed $70-$78 range.
Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion.
The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for fast-growing AI sector. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to publicly sell its shares.
Vast amounts of money have been poured into AI infrastructure and the development of AI based tools. But questions are being raised over whether and when those investments will pay off.
The seven founders, who set up Anthropic up in 2021, will become multi-billionaires immediately.
The firm's $1.5tn valuation makes it more valuable than Walmart and Samsung and on almost on a par with Tesla and Meta.
But strong demand could push its share price, and overall valuation, higher, once shares are publicly traded.
One early investor in the company who spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymity, said the original sale was heavily oversubscribed, with demand ten times the number of shares available.
Anthropic's revenues have ballooned in the last year, to $33bn in the nine months to September this year, as the market for its tools, designed to speed up processes including coding, writing and digesting information, has grown.
But net losses have also increased, reaching $104bn for the same period, according to the company's IPO document.
Leah Bramwell from Canaccord Wealth said there had been strong interest in Anthropic shares "across the board" including both institutional and retail - that is private individual - investors, which she said suggested it was not simply a "retail-driven frenzy into into AI names".
In total Anthropic could raise $107bn. Over $81bn comes from the public share sale, with an additional $26bn from separate investments from a group of tech firms including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
Anthropic could raise a further $12bn through an additional provision, which is normal practice, to permit further shares to be sold if demand is very high.
Elon Musk's SpaceX raised an initial $75bn in its IPO in June this year.
The company soared in value when it joined the Nasdaq, reaching $2.2tn, although in the weeks that followed, the share price fell.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei co-founded firm five years ago
OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year. Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology.
While there is excitement around Anthropic's listing, there is also some concern from investors about its future ability to generate profits in a competitive area.
Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue was whether it could "keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.
However, the share sale would give investors "direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity", Wang said.
Anthropic was started by seven former OpenAI employees, led by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei.
Dario Amodei has been outspoken about the risks posed by AI, amounting in his view to a possible threat to human existence.
The company has called for a slowdown in the development of AI, and a greater focus on safeguards while forging ahead with plans to grow quickly and boost its financing through the public markets.
OpenAI has voiced similar sentiments and delayed its plans to list on the stock market in order to address AI safety concerns.
Technology stocks have lost value in recent weeks following the US midterm elections. Democrats, who now control of both chambers of Congress, are expected to be tougher on AI regulation. Some Democrat candidates opposed the rapid build of data centres required to run AI.
But Anthropic went ahead with its market listing, despite the market volatility, because it needed to tap into additional funds, said Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower.
"AI is financially demanding," Norton told the BBC. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more and so the time has come."
Expensive computer chips, necessary for the industry to operate, are in short supply.
And the US Federal Reserve is concerned about high AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss interest rates, as well as the high concentration of AI exposure among a small number of firms.

Bayern Munich boss Vincent Kompany says he is "very healthy" and grateful for all of the support he has received as he prepares to return to the dugout on Friday.
The 40-year-old former Manchester City captain was taken to hospital after falling ill while watching the club's second team train last month.
Kompany was diagnosed with meningeal irritation - an inflammation of the protective membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
Speaking at a news conference on Thursday he thanked the club, medical staff, players, coaches and fans for their support.
"At the time, it was a new experience. Looking back, everything went perfectly. I received support right away, from the club and the doctors. I'm very grateful.
"You try to stay calm and wait until you have the results. It was a positive process, all the tests were positive.
"I have to say, I'm very healthy. We did a lot of tests, and they all came back fine. In those quiet moments, you also try to learn.
"Now I feel very good again and I'm happy to be back with the team."
While he has been recovering Kompany's assistant Aaron Danks has led the side to four wins and a draw.
"I'd also like to thank the coaching community," Kompany added. "We're always competing, but almost every coach has reached out to me, even if we've played against each other and perhaps argued as well. That's a beautiful thing."
Bayern, for whom England captain Harry Kane has been in fine form, are top of the Bundesliga, level on points with Borussia Dortmund.
Defending champions Bayern face Cologne on Friday after the end of the two-week international break.

The console’s latest update finally activates its dormant Wi-Fi hardware enabling a handful of new features.
Analogue has long been good at expanding the features and functionality of its consoles through regular firmware updates, but installing those updates has always required moving files around with a memory card. That’s no longer the case with the Analogue 3D , the company’s modernized version of the Nintendo 64. Although the console has had Wi-Fi hardware since day one, it’s only now been finally activated through the last update you’ll need to install with a memory card.
Analogue released the version 1.6.0 firmware for the Analogue 3D yesterday which adds support for 2.4GHz, 5GHz, mixed, and hidden Wi-Fi networks. Once the update is installed the Wi-Fi setup process will begin automatically when the console is booted, but there’s now an added Wi-Fi section in the Analogue 3D’s settings menu for updating passwords and other details later.
The console’s new Wi-Fi capabilities add a couple of useful features at launch. In the future the Analogue 3D will be able to download and install firmware updates so it automatically keeps itself up to date. The new wireless capabilities enable automatic date and time settings based on your time zone, too, and in the privacy section of the console’s settings menu you’ll now find an option for sharing “anonymous usage and analytics data” with Analogue to help further improve its hardware.

Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq Thursday after pricing its IPO at $83 per share, valuing the artificial intelligence giant at $1.5 trillion and surpassing SpaceX as the largest initial public offering on record. The IPO puts to the test Wall Street's faith in ​the AI boom, pitting promises of the technology as an economic game-changer against fears of a market bubble and risks to humanity.
Anthropic launched its blockbuster initial public offering on Thursday, smashing records and eclipsing SpaceX 's June listing to become the largest IPO ever.
The higher-than-anticipated pricing – at $83 per share – signals broad investor enthusiasm for AI stocks even amid some market uncertainty stemming from the departure of Nvidia 's CEO and worries about an AI bubble.
But the bigger test will be how Anthropic fares on the stock market.
Read more Anthropic files for mammoth IPO as revenues and losses mount
Anthropic said the offering consists of 980 million shares, roughly 956 million sold by the company and the rest by selling stockholders. Proceeds totaling $81 billion put Anthropic's IPO ahead of SpaceX , which raised about $75 billion in June.
SpaceX, however, holds a higher valuation, about $1.9 trillion as of Wednesday afternoon.

Anthropic decided to barrel ahead with the IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public.
Then there's the spectacular downfall of one of the industry's biggest cheerleaders, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

“This is strong appetite for this major AI IPO in Anthropic, and it’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia. The pricing shows strong demand among investors,” said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co.
The company’s rival, OpenAI , is not planning to go public until next year.
Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings as “substantial”. Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited.
While the company has ample cash for now, it will likely run through it quickly if it cannot raise more soon, given its outsize spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend $900 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion in the next 12 months.
An IPO is essentially a way to raise money, instead of going into further debt. And borrowing has gotten more expensive. That’s partly due to inflation fears and partly due to the sector’s massive cash needs, which have drawn comparisons to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads.
Lenders fear that AI companies have taken on too much debt to expand while having no clear path to profitability.
Anthropic's IPO also means its employees can begin to sell their vested stock, a payout that will make many of them millionaires. The IPO could also give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion and potentially add billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela Amodei.
Watch more Concerns mount over artificial intelligence as Silicon Valley sees AI boom
Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google , startups in the US and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business.
Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all lost more money than they’ve made because of the huge costs associated with building AI. That has fuelled growing concerns about a bubble forming in the sector.
Dario Amodei cautioned in September that the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned, AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the internet within months.
Amid those fears, the regulatory environment could also change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a backlash against data centres. And two big states offering incentives for data centres, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democratic governors vowing to stop new construction.
Watch more US voters reject AI data centres: Could the backlash spread to France?
Adding to the pressure is the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse. Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently.

Watching fights wasn’t as good as practical experience, but it got the mice halfway there.
There’s something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it’s the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout. Scientists have debated whether watching violent things could make us more aggressive, but it could also be an adaptive survival strategy. Male mice, for instance, who watch other mice fighting learned enough about how to fight to better protect themselves (compared to mice who didn’t watch fights) when pitted against stronger, more aggressive opponents, according to a paper published in the journal Nature.
The team assigned male mice randomly to three different groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training involving three 10-minute sessions per day. The novices played with stuffed mice in isolation, while the spectators watched various pairs of fighter mice battle it out from a raised platform behind a transparent barrier—a set-up chosen to let them smell and listen to the fights as well as observe them.
The ninth day was “fight night,” when all the mice had to face a daunting opponent in three 4-minute rounds. Each fight was filmed from above so that the mouse behavior could be analyzed. To monitor corresponding changes in brain activity, the team engineered the rodents’ excitatory brain cells to glow green whenever they were activated, while inhibitory brain cells glowed red. They also implanted tiny optical fibers into 12 interconnected brain regions so they could track changing activity in every brain region simultaneously.
How did they get the mice to fight? “Mice are naturally territorial,” co-author Jorge Iravedra-Garcia of Princeton University told Ars. “A traditional behavioral assay that experimenters use is called resident intruder. You just drop mice that are bred to be slightly weaker, and a little bit more docile, into the home cage of strains we know are more on the aggressive side. Those strains are typically very good at just naturally evoking that behavior.”
So the fights weren’t entirely fair. “We tip the scales in favor of having a clear winner and a clear loser by having the clear winner be at home, be bigger, and be more experienced,” co-author Annegret Falkner, also of Princeton, told Ars. “We really wanted to show that these changes are adaptive in some way. Animals don’t know what the outcome of a fight is before they enter it. So we set up a situation where the outcome is a little bit more uncertain for the mouse.”
The results: the spectator mice ended up being better prepared for fight night—despite being weaker, less aggressive strains—because they watched fighter mice during the training sessions. Specifically, both spectators and fighters spent less time with their backs turned toward opponents than novice mice, and were also quicker to attack. They also used similar moves. Granted, they weren’t quite as skilled as their fighter-mouse brethren; practical experience still mattered. But they learned enough through observation to perform better than the novices.
That behavioral change was mirrored in the neural data: the brains of the spectator mice altered to more closely resemble the brains of the fighting mice across all 12 of the interconnected regions. During training, the spectator inhibitory cells resembled a fighter’s, while the excitatory cells were closer to those of novice mice, but that changed on fight night, when both types of cells more closely resembled those of fighting mice.
“When you’re watching a fight, you’re paying attention to many things at once,” said Iravedra-Garcia. “You’re not just simulating that aggressive behavior in your head, you’re also trying to gauge who’s dangerous, who’s not, who’s actually involved in the fight versus ‘Do I know them? Are they novel to me?’ Witnessing aggression leaves a circuit trace that changes how an animal behaves in its next conflict, and that trace looks similar to the one left by fighting itself.”
“They can watch males walking around all they want and none of this happens,” said Falkner. “There’s something specifically salient and arousing about attack that makes them both want to attend to it and also drives this specific plasticity mechanism. That’s one of the open questions: why is attack so sticky? Probably because it creates these adaptive behavioral changes.”
There have been similar studies, notably with macaques . According to Falkner, this latest study adds to that body of research by pointing to a specific mechanism for the learned behavior. “There’s this broad decrease in regions that are known to provide inhibitory control for some of these aggression control networks,” she said. “This one piece of the aggression network is really just the tip of the iceberg in terms of how global networks for aggression control respond during these observed activities. I think these subcortical subnetworks are really recurrent. It’s a tiny piece of a larger network .”
It’s an open question whether such findings involving mice could extend to human beings. “Although it’s difficult to draw a one-to-one parallel, these circuits are extremely conserved, especially these brain regions that seem to show this robust change in inhibitory tone,” said Falkner. “We think about violence as being maladaptive in human culture, but if you are a mouse or an animal who’s around a lot of aggression, it’s actually highly adaptive for you to be ready to fight at any particular time.” The same could be true of humans.
The authors plan to extend their research to determine whether female mice watching male mice duking it out changes their mating preferences. They also want to try to artificially induce the same brain activity changes and corresponding behavior. “It doesn’t seem that farfetched to me,” said Falkner. “I think we know the state that the circuit needs to be in to execute this particular behavioral strategy. So whatever pattern of stimulation we can use to kick this plasticity mechanism into gear seems reasonable.”
DOI: Nature, 2026. 10.1038/s41586-026-11217-9 ( About DOIs ).

The music industry will not accept an AI carveout deal that leaves other creative sectors behind, rejecting a reported proposal to give musicians special treatment while allowing big tech to train on other copyrighted material – described by David Pocock as a “divide and conquer strategy”.
The trade union representing writers and creatives is “alarmed” at a proposal to let AI companies train on Australian data if they buy a permit, an idea also strongly rebuffed by the Coalition and Greens.
The Albanese government would not comment on the reported proposal, but senior ministers have raised concerns about current copyright law in recent days, hinting reforms were needed.

“I can’t see any creative workers leaving their colleagues behind,” Pullen said.
The Australian Financial Review reported on Thursday the government was considering a copyright change under which AI companies would buy permits to train on Australian content, but that music may be exempted. Such a proposal would be more in line with AI companies, after Anthropic suggested a model of “conditional approval” to scrape content unless a rightsholder objected, and OpenAI told a parliamentary committee it would “potentially” support paying into a fund for creators.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
Guardian Australia was not able to independently verify details of the proposal. One senior member of the creative community, involved in copyright discussions with government, said they had heard some details of such an idea, but others said they had not and doubted the Albanese government would seriously entertain it. One source in the AI industry, who declined to be named, said they would welcome such a plan.
Herd said she was unaware of the proposal before Thursday, but the music industry would not desert other creatives.
“Had we been consulted, we would have advised this scheme is unnecessary, unworkable and designed to suit the commercial interests of AI companies, not protect creators,” she told Guardian Australia.
“Our position is unchanged: we stand with the rest of the creative and media industries.”
Herd and Pullen said such a scheme would be difficult to implement technically, questioning how content like movies or TV shows – which combine copyrighted elements such as music, video and screenwriting – would be treated if just one element was exempted from AI scraping.
“This just seems like such a convoluted path, when AI companies have had an open invitation to sit down and negotiate for years. We have been working with government to come up with a model since 2024. We’ve come up with solutions and tech has steadfastly refused to even talk,” Pullen said.
While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese , has declared it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, and that artists “need to be compensated”, some AI companies have argued it is too difficult to make individual licensing deals under existing copyright law.
The Media, Entertainment & Arts Alliance said it would be “alarmed” at the reported proposal, and demanded protections promised by Albanese “must apply to all creative sectors”.
While government MPs declined to comment on the report, senior Labor figures have recently begun more forcefully pointing to what they claim are shortfalls in copyright law in the AI age – despite major rightsholder groups rejecting the need for change . The industry minister, Tim Ayres, on Tuesday said “the status quo is no good” for creative workers, a line repeated by the acting prime minister, Richard Marles, on Thursday. Marles added on News24: “People are being ripped off”.
The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, also used newly strengthened language when contacted, promising “certainty and strong protections for Australian artists”.
“Right now, the work of Australian creatives is being used without their consent or payment,” a spokesperson for Rowland said.
“The Government has long advocated for tech companies to strike commercial deals with Australian artists, and we will continue to do so.”
Potentially carving out musicians did not win support among parliamentarians, either.
The shadow attorney general, Michaelia Cash, claimed such a proposal would “divide the rightsholders”.
“This ham-fisted tactic should be strongly resisted. Everyone who owns property should have the same right for it not to be stolen.”
Pocock also described it as “some sort of divide and conquer strategy”.
“It’s hard to know what [Labor] are actually doing at the moment. The joint select committee hasn’t even given its report to the government, and we’re hearing all sorts of whispers about what the government is planning.”
Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young urged the government not to meet copyright demands requested by big tech.
“What they’re asking Australia to do actually is to undermine copyright the world over. Australia will become known as the Cayman Islands for AI if we allow this loophole to happen,” she told News24.

PRESS REVIEW – Thursday, November 19: An historic trilateral summit takes place in Shenzhen between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin. But is it more optics than substance? Also, a highly awaited decision from the International Court of Justice could redefine genocide. Finally, a huge cultural moment: "Grand Theft Auto VI" is out and the reviews are ecstatic.
Donald Trump , Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet in Shenzhen this Thursday for an historic trilateral gathering on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Libération, the French left-wing paper, calls them the "infernal throuple" and wonders if this is an historic meeting or a meeting about optics. Arend van Dam, a Dutch cartoonist, thinks Putin and Xi are just paying lip service to Trump in a front-page cartoon published by Le Monde. British daily the Guardian evokes a "new world order" while La Repubblica, the Italian daily, calls the summit "global disorder."
In Asia, the South China Morning Post notes that Trump received an unprecedented welcome when he touched down on Wednesday. Xi greeted him at the airport – the first time in seven decades that a China leader has done so, the paper reports. The Taipei Times says Taiwan is closely watching the talks. Relations with China are extremely tense – Beijing has ramped up military pressure on the island to which it lays claim and Russia sent two military aircraft down Taiwan's east coast recently, the paper reports. The US is Taiwan's most important international backer.
Elsewhere, the International Court of Justice will deliver a verdict this Thursday on whether Myanmar is guilty of genocide in the persecution of the Rohingya people, a Muslim minority group. According to the UN, some 10,000 Rohingya have been killed and dozens of villages destroyed by the Myanmar government. Since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948 after the Holocaust, individuals have been successfully prosecuted for genocide in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia . But if convicted, Myanmar would become the first country to be found guilty of genocide and such a ruling would also define what constitutes the intention of committing a genocide and what proof is needed to show that it has occurred. The verdict is even more crucial as South Africa in 2023 accused Israel of violating the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. That decision will not be handed down before the end of this decade.
Finally, we end with the biggest cultural event of the year, at least for gamers: "Grand Theft Auto VI" has been released, to huge accolades. The Guardian evokes a "tonal shift" for the game famous for its "violence, misanthropy and pitch-black humour." The new romance is a Bonnie and Clyde-style love story. For those who fear the romance might tone down the grittiness of the game, rest assured, GTA is still "absurdly foul-mouthed, filthy and over-the-top offensive", the paper says.
Variety magazine reports that the game already has a score of 99 on Metacritic, tying it for the highest-rated game of all time with the original 1998 Nintendo 64 version of "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time". With reviews like that, it is no surprise that many workers around the world will be mysteriously calling in sick this Thursday. Parents, teachers, schools and HR departments will be managing a flood of sick calls and unexcused absences. According to The New York Times , there is even a term for it: "GTA flu". One Silicon Valley company has offered a floating day off – since studies show that playing video games improves productivity and reduces anxiety. But one Scottish man has taken it a step further. The Scottish Sun reports that he paid his wife and daughter to sign a "non-interference" contract – and stocked up on snacks so that he can game uninterrupted for the next seven days!
You can catch our press review every morning on France 24 at 7:20am and 9:20am (Paris time), from Monday to Friday.

Australian physicists chose to transmit the word ‘gravity’ in binary code through brick wall
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Australian scientists have used gravity as a means of communication, in a proof-of-concept experiment involving a snail-paced 1950s elevator, a brick wall and a men’s bathroom.
Physicists at the University of Queensland have used gravity to transmit a “practically unblockable” message about 70cm through a brick wall, by sending an elevator up and down between two floors and measuring changes in the gravitational field as a result of the movement.
The research, published in the journal Science Advances , involved a sensitive detection device known as a gravimeter, which was set up on the floor of a men’s bathroom adjacent to the lift.
The gravimeter was able to detect the position of the elevator’s 1.8-tonne counterweight as it moved between two levels – representing 0 and 1 in binary code – which enabled the scientists to send a message.
The researchers chose to transmit the word “gravity”, or 1000111 1110010 1100001 1110110 1101001 1110100 1111001 in binary code. At a transmission rate of one bit (digit) per minute, the single word took nearly an hour to send.
The scientists say that while gravitational communication is currently far from usable given its extremely slow speed, an advantage is that it is a “practically unblockable wireless communication scheme”.
“Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” said co-author Dr Charles Woffinden, of UQ’s school of mathematics and physics, in a statement. “Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with wifi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.”
Study co-author Prof Matthew Davis told Guardian Australia: “At the moment, it’s very hard to imagine how it could be practically useful.” But he added that the experiment was “theoretically interesting enough that it was worth doing”.
To put into perspective how slow the message transmission was, Davis said that Nasa’s Voyager 1 spacecraft, which after 49 years of travel had just reached a distance of one light-day away, could “communicate with Earth at a faster data rate than our communication concept”.
According to Davis, the new method of communicating could theoretically occur at ranges of up to 500 metres and at a rate 15 times faster, if more sensitive quantum gravity sensors were used.
The idea for the elevator study arose from a project to develop a contactless weighbridge – which would use quantum sensors to detect changes in the strength of gravity due to a passing truck, allowing scientists to determine the mass of a large vehicle.
Classical gravimeters can be thought of as a mass on a spring. “If you stretch the spring, the mass bounces up and down at a certain rate, which is determined by the spring and the gravitational field,” Davis said. “If the gravitational field changes ever so slightly, the rate at which it bounces back and forth changes.”
“Sometimes doing physics leads in unexpected ways and it’s a bit of fun … you get to do quirky things on the side,” he added. “It’s one of the great joys of science to have stuff like this happen.”
Other near-unblockable methods of communication – involving neutrinos or gravitational waves – have been proposed, “but these approaches are somewhat hindered by the difficulty in generating a measurable signal”, the scientists note.
The physicists conducted the research in UQ’s Parnell physics building, which is also home to the world’s longest-running science experiment – the pitch drop experiment , which began in 1927.

As Google steps up its competition with Apple in the item-tracking market, smaller brands are also looking to carve out a piece of the category. The latest entrant is Nimble , the sustainable accessories brand best known for its charging products.
Founded in 2018 by former Mophie executives, the California-based company announced Thursday that it’s expanding into the category with “Trace,” a seven-product collection of item trackers designed to blend tracking technology into everyday accessories.
Nimble’s new collection arrives as competition in the Bluetooth tracking market continues to heat up. Apple’s AirTag helped popularize the category, while Google recently introduced its first-party tracker, the $29 Pixel Tag, powered by its Find Hub network. Meanwhile, established third-party players, such as Chipolo and Pebblebee , continue to expand their lineups.
Nimble is taking a slightly different approach. Rather than introducing another standalone tracker to attach to a set of keys or slip into a bag, the company has integrated tracking technology directly into practical accessories, including wallets, keychains, luggage tags, and passport covers.
The lineup includes seven products, ranging from the $14.95 Trace Tag, which features a replaceable coin-cell battery, to the $49.95 Trace Folio, a passport cover with built-in rechargeable tracking. Other options include the Trace Keyfob ($19.95), Trace Slim Wallet Card ($29.95), Trace Keychain ($29.95), Trace Luggage Tag ($39.95), and Trace Wallet ($39.95).
The entire collection is compatible with both Apple’s Find My and Google’s Find Hub networks.
Ross Howe, co-founder and CEO of Nimble, told us that the company’s approach is designed to differentiate its products from traditional trackers.
“Most locators are built as utility gadgets, not as things you want to own. Few were asking why the locator couldn’t just be the nice object itself. So, for example, we made a wallet findable instead of making a tracker that fits a wallet. We also thought more options should be rechargeable.”
The Trace Luggage Tag and Trace Folio are arguably the most interesting products in the collection. Dedicated luggage tags and passport covers with built-in tracking remain relatively uncommon, giving Nimble an opportunity to stand out in a market. There are only a few alternatives, including Spotminder’s $59 passport cover with Apple Find My support, which is $10 more than Nimble’s option. Knog Scout offers a luggage tag, although I find its design a little too bulky.
Rechargeability is another appealing aspect of Nimble’s new collection. Several models support USB-C or wireless charging, offering an alternative to the disposable batteries found in many traditional trackers. Howe says battery life lasts for “months,” with the Trace Keyfob, for example, rated for approximately six months on a charge.
Sustainability is another major part of Nimble’s pitch. Staying true to its roots, the company has incorporated eco-friendly materials throughout the collection, including recycled plastics and plant-based, vegan aloe leather. The products have also undergone third-party testing for chemicals of concern.
“We’ve spent the last two years going through the chemistry of our products line by line to remove or limit as many harmful ingredients as possible. Trace is the first collection designed specifically to meet these higher standards. We’re not 100% yet, but the independent labs checking our work will help us get there,” Howe said.
The collection is available now through its website and Amazon. All seven products come in five color options: Black, Stone, Tangerine, Plum, and Teal.

Productivity apps are simultaneously trying to feed more context to their AI tools while also making those AI assistants available in every nook and corner of their products. Superhuman (formerly Grammarly) is going in the same direction with the rollout of features, including a personalized Go assistant, making agents available in Docs, and third-party agent integrations.
While some of the company’s AI features have faced criticism , Superhuman started pushing its Go assistant after its rebranding last year . With the new rollout, it is making Go learn context across different apps and give better personalized suggestions for prompts. Superhuman is revamping its onboarding flow to let users connect their preferred tools and load context about their work upfront.
The assistant works inline with the cursor — just like Grammarly does — and also manages other agents. Superhuman is also making the agent proactive, which means it looks for your schedule, keeps an eye on your email, and even drafts responses. The updated Go agent also learns users’ writing styles and responds accordingly in email and Docs.
The productivity company is adding 20 new connected agents, including DeepL, Legora, Amplitude, Databricks, and Blackboard, through its Go SDK.
The company is also thinking about adding AI to different products, including Docs and Superhuman Mail. In Docs, all Go agents work natively, and you can set them off to work on different tasks in the background. Users can also set routines to trigger workflows based on events.
Until now, Mail has used AI as its central tool, which is being replaced by Go. Users can also do enterprise search by using data from the company knowledge base and connected tools. Go also uses this context to form drafts and organize the inbox across Google and Outlook accounts.
Superhuman acquired notetaker Fathom in September to add more context to its suite. The company is now rolling out live collaborative notetaking, which would be shared across the team. Plus, Go can now make decisions post-meeting, like forming an initial draft of a proposal.
The company’s CEO, Shishir Mehrotra, said that Go has had good momentum with over 1 million active users. There are a host of agents now that are vying for users’ attention on both the personal and professional front. Mehrotra thinks that while Go is more work-focused, it can help with personal emails and schedules.
“One of the reasons why these assistants have been popular is that they treat you as a whole person and recognize that we need to cover both extremes. Go is definitely more work-focused than some of the tools coming out of the pure consumer ecosystem. It doesn’t mean we draw the boundary at helping you with your personal tasks or helping you with your calendar or all of your email,” he told TechCrunch over a call.
While Go might not directly compete with the likes of Instinct, Muse, and Fo, Superhuman wants users to choose its assistant over something like OpenAI’s Dots or Claude Duet.

Google is teaming up with Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin to launch its AI server satellites. The companies announced on Thursday that Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket will shuttle satellites equipped with Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) into space in the first quarter of 2029.
The partnership is part of Google’s Project Suncatcher, a moonshot plan that could eventually put AI data centers in space. Google deployed its first AI server satellite in October, successfully booting up its TPUs and using the onboard Gemma 4 model to transmit an AI-generated haiku to Earth .

“We also have a responsibility to not go too fast and cut too many corners.”
NASA recently announced a significant shakeup to the Artemis program that will land humans on the Moon.
The moves were designed to give the agency’s lunar lander providers—SpaceX with its Starship vehicle, and Blue Origin with Blue Moon—more flexibility in reaching the Moon. For Starship, this means docking with Orion in Earth orbit, and then traveling to the Moon in tandem. For Blue Moon, it shifts the rendezvous with Orion all the way to low-lunar orbit.
These changes benefit the lunar landers, but in turn impose more of a burden on the Orion spacecraft, which is built for NASA by Lockheed Martin. To understand the implications for the spacecraft, Ars spoke with Kirk Shireman, Human Spaceflight Exploration and Orion program manager at Lockheed.
For Starship, the evolved plan has SpaceX fueling a Starship lunar lander in low-Earth orbit before docking with Orion in high-Earth orbit. The crew will fly to the Moon on board Orion before two of the four astronauts transfer into Starship for a landing on the Moon.
Due to the docking configuration with Starship, Orion must now fly backward to the Moon, with its Service Module at the top of the stack. This is a fundamentally different flying posture than Orion was designed for, Shireman said, and creates issues for Orion’s propulsion system.
As a result, the Service Module, which is provided by the European Space Agency, will require modifications to its propellant tanks. This is because liquid propellant would move toward the gas inlet side of the tanks, rather than settling in the direction expected during normal operation.
“When you push it the other way, the liquid goes to the gas end of the tank, and you don’t want the liquid in the gas part,” Shireman said. “Bad things can happen to you.” To address this, he said, the European Space Agency and its main contractor, Airbus, are modifying the vehicle’s tanks for Starship lunar missions.
NASA and Lockheed engineers have also been studying the impact of increased acceleration on Orion when the vehicle is attached to Starship. Under Orion’s original mission architecture, the spacecraft would experience accelerations of about 0.1 to 0.15 g during the translunar injection burn, Shireman said. But with Starship providing the thrust, the acceleration would increase to approximately 0.8 to 1 g, acting in the opposite direction from the one originally planned.
Orion’s structure must be certified to handle a substantially higher acceleration in the opposite direction, Shireman said.
Before astronauts land on the Moon, NASA is also planning a mission in low-Earth orbit to test Orion’s interactions with the lunar landers. Shireman said this change in plans for Artemis III, announced earlier this year, has created new hazards, as Orion was not designed to spend more than a short period of time in low-Earth orbit.
Heating is a concern, he said, because Orion was designed for deep space, which is colder than the thermal environment closer to Earth. For example, he said, Orion has passive thermal features designed to prevent the spacecraft from getting too cold in deep space. One of these is a silver-looking exterior tape that dissipates electrical charge and limits the radiation of heat into space. As a result, some of this tape will be removed for the Artemis III mission.
Engineers are also analyzing how to manage electrical loads to reduce heating and protect the avionics and crew cabin.
Another big change that stems from spending approximately two weeks in low-Earth orbit is the orbital debris environment, which is more congested than in deep space. Shireman said NASA and Lockheed have not completed their assessment of the orbital-debris risk associated with the new mission profile. This should be done by January, and, if the risks are too high, it might lead to modifications of Orion’s orbit for the mission.
“There’s going to be a higher risk from an MMOD standpoint,” Shireman said of orbital debris near Earth. “It’ll be higher risk than flying out to the Moon.”
Earlier this year, NASA removed the lunar landing from Artemis III, turning the mission into a demonstration of rendezvous and docking operations in low-Earth orbit. The agency is now targeting 2027 for the mission, leaving Orion and the lunar landing companies with a compressed schedule to complete substantial technical integration work.
This may seem like a fairly straightforward process, but docking is rather complex. It involves mechanical capabilities like hooks, connectors, and pins; there are thruster-plume interactions with the landers, including possible damage from hot or abrasive exhaust; concerns about whether Orion’s laser system might incorrectly interpret reflections from surfaces on Starship or Blue Moon; and more.
“We were going to do that work, but not on Artemis III, and not for both of the landers,” Shireman said of docking with Starship and Blue Moon. “It was going to be spaced out, so all that work gets crunched into this time frame.”
Lockheed is working closely with NASA to prepare Orion to maintain an Artemis III schedule for a launch in summer or fall of 2027.
“We’re working three shifts,” Shireman said. “We had a zero margin schedule already, so we’re, I call it hand-to-hand combat. Literally every day we’re clawing to see, ‘Hey, can we save a shift here? Can we save half a shift there?’”
Shireman said he supports the urgency of Isaacman and NASA in their contest with China over the Moon. But it is important to keep an eye on mission safety, said Shireman, who worked at NASA during both the Challenger and Columbia accidents.
“We also have a responsibility to not go too fast and cut too many corners and make sure that we are not taking undue risks,” he said.

When Heather Champion raised a council motion in March opposing a massive new gas plant to power a large datacentre in the Southern Highlands of New South Wales, it failed to pass.
Five months later, when the local councillor for Wingecaribee raised a new motion calling for the federal government to implement a moratorium on new datacentres, it passed unanimously.
“I think the council’s change in perspective is a direct result of the change in sentiment in the community,” Champion says.
The shift highlights grassroots successes in pushing back on datacentre construction and how those wins are inspiring other communities to take similar action.
In May, Guardian Australia reported on three datacentre projects across the country – Hazelmere in Western Australia, West Footscray in Victoria, and Lane Cove in New South Wales.
Since the report, the project proposals have been withdrawn in WA and NSW , and NextDC’s M3 expansion in West Footscray has been stalled after Jemena, the power provider, delayed the installation of taller power poles after the community outcry.
Lane Cove Responsible Planning spokesperson, Sasha Titchkosky, says after the success of having the Goodman Group’s Mars datacentre in Lane Cove withdrawn, she is working with communities in western Sydney and the Southern Highlands on their own campaigns.
Titchkosky says by working together, the groups send a strong signal to industry and politicians that they need to do better.
As it stands, councils play a role in approving datacentres in some states, but in others, such as NSW and Victoria, fast-tracked approvals skip the local council stage. The federal government has proposed rules that would from next year set mandatory minimum requirements for large datacentres, including how projects manage energy, water, costs, community engagement, location and workforce impacts.
“Just saying they’re going to put in place regulations, but still allowing datacentres to be approved … isn’t good enough.
“They [need to] either put a pause on approvals or basically say that everyone who gets approved now will be subject to the regulations when they come in force.”
Campaigners across Australia are sharing notes and tips through WhatsApp, using the platform to organise rallies and discuss new proposals.
In Victoria, a community wiki site displays a map of locations of datacentre proposals, the community groups organising around them, and links to campaign tips from US groups that successfully lobbied against the sector in the recent midterm elections.
Titchkosky has been in contact with campaigners in the Southern Highlands, where an application refusal for one of three gas plants capable of producing 673MW of power in total is being challenged in the NSW land and environment court. The applicant, Cloud Carrier, wants to use the gas plant to power a “data campus” in Moss Vale with AI “at its core”.
“We are sharing skills, messages – it’s very lateral and it’s very informal,” Champion says of the community networks’ organic growth.
They share what works and what doesn’t work – and what might work in one area may not be suitable in another, she says.
“[Lane Cove’s] circumstances are just so completely different but in some ways that’s been really helpful … having [our] voices combined does provide some breadth.”
The groups are also working with communities in western Sydney to build their capacity to take on new centres planned for the area.
Mandy Ottaviano, a masters of sustainability student at the University of Sydney who has been researching community action against datacentres in Australia says there is a “real desire” for the groups to connect with each other, but there is no formal organisation.
“What we’re not seeing a lot of yet is [non-government organisations] stepping in and bridging that gap in terms of coordinating those groups in a meaningful way together,” she says.
“We haven’t yet seen any emergence of a national kind of coalition.”
The chief executive officer for Data Centres Australia, Belinda Dennett, acknowledges there is “more interest from the community” in datacentre development than ever before, and datacentre companies are stepping up community consultation.
“This ranges from community information sessions, door knocking, newsletters, websites, hotline phone numbers and social media updates,” Dennett says.
“Third parties delivering energy, broadband and water infrastructure are also an important part of building community support so we also encourage more coordination and information sharing between parties.”
While state and federal governments appear to be reacting to the growing community concerns over datacentres – some states are introducing new rules and the federal government is set to follow suit early next year – campaigners are concerned the changes don’t go far enough.
The New South Wales parliament’s long-running inquiry into datacentres released its report earlier this month , with the committee voting to remove two contentious recommendations: that the NSW government advocates for a moratorium on new datacentre developments until new obligations are in place; and to advocate for the new federal rules to be applied retrospectively.
The chair, Greens MP Abigail Boyd, was the only committee member to vote in support of the recommendations.
“It appears that both the Labor and Liberal parties remain in hock to the industry talking points,” Boyd said in the chair’s foreword in the report.
“I was particularly disappointed that both Labor and Liberal parties voted together against a pause on data centre approvals until sufficiently robust and legally binding obligations are in place, and similarly voted against advocating for data centres currently in the planning pipeline to have to comply with any rules that are currently being contemplated.”
Boyd said the delay to the rules coming in federally “makes clear the coordinated effort by governments and industry to avoid having to comply with even the most moderate of environmental and social obligations”.
Champion says she was “really frustrated” the recommendations were removed.
“We agreed between the group of us we would call for a moratorium, and all the community groups know that’s what’s needed.
Titchkosky says it is “clear as day where the two major parties” sit on datacentres – and questions whether the move may prove politically destructive, given datacentre disquiet played a pivotal role in voter sentiment in the US midterms.
“They’re ultimately prepared to sell out communities for multinational corporate interests,” she says. “I think we are going to see the same issues play out in Victoria and NSW in our upcoming elections as they were in the US midterms.

In case filed at the ICJ in 2019, The Gambia accused Myanmar of breaching the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The United Nations’ top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Muslim minority Rohingya population.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) at The Hague delivered its judgement on Thursday about the military crackdown that drove more than 730,000 mainly Muslim Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh.
ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar “has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention”.
It is the first time a state has been found responsible for genocide at the court. The ruling marked only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the crime had been committed.
The case was brought by the West African nation of The Gambia, which in 2019 accused Myanmar of seeking to destroy the Rohingya people. It asked the ICJ to rule that Myanmar breached the 1948 Genocide Convention, order it to end any illegal activities targeting the Rohingya and ensure those responsible for genocide are punished.
Myanmar claimed its crackdown was in response to attacks on police posts by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA).
Evidence shows Myanmar forces killed 10,000 Rohingya, Iwasawa said during a three-hour readout of the verdict.
“The Court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya ⁠⁠civilians, perpetrated widespread acts ⁠⁠of sexual violence as well as acts of ⁠⁠extreme violence against children and ⁠⁠attacked fleeing Rohingya ⁠⁠as they sought to flee in large numbers to ‌‌Bangladesh,” he added.
In specific cases that he referred to, he said Myanmar had acted with “genocidal intent”.
The ICJ said that the “only reasonable inference” from evidence of widespread atrocities by Myanmar security forces is that they had the intent to destroy a “substantial part” of the Rohingya minority.
It said Myanmar should have known that there was a risk of genocide when armed civilians participated in the military campaign. “Myanmar thus violated its obligation to prevent genocide,” it added.
Myanmar is now obliged to provide reparations and restitution “as a result of Myanmar’s wrongful acts”, Iwasawa said.
The court said appropriate restitution by Myanmar would include: Facilitating the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya; returning or replacing all collective property damaged; facilitating the search for the disappeared and ensuring proper burials; providing for the physical and psychological rehabilitation of those mentally injured; and ensuring the population’s protection from persecution.
The court established that at least four genocidal acts have been proven, said Al Jazeera’s Step Vaessen, reporting from the Hague. They are the mass killing of civilians; the forced displacement of hundreds of thousands of people; serious harm inflicted upon the group; and the prevention of birth.
The Rohingya have long been treated as second-class citizens, well before 2017, according to the judge, Vaessen said. They were also forced to take part in a birth control programme, she added.
“So the judge really saw this as a very strong explanation that … a genocidal act was committed there.”
The verdict is “extremely important for the Rohingya,” our correspondent said. “They’ve been waiting for 10 years for any kind of justice, but it’s also important for the whole international community because genocide is such a difficult act to prove.”
The hardest part of any genocide case is proving specific intent to destroy a group in whole or in part – an extremely high bar – said Toby Cadman, an international human rights lawyer. He noted that the ICJ had never before ruled that a state has specific intent to commit genocide.
“The court is guided by the genocide convention and what the genocide convention states and it is a high threshold,” Cadman told Al Jazeera.
Human rights organisations welcomed the judgement. “We hope this ruling marks the beginning of a long overdue process of accountability in Myanmar,” Amnesty International said in a statement. It added that all crimes under international law “must be effectively investigated and those suspected of responsibility brought to justice”.
Cadman said that the situation does not come to an end with the ICJ’s ruling and a lot will depend on what comes next. This includes whether the issue goes before the UN Security Council and whether there are sanctions, or other remedies that the court can order to ensure it is enforced.
More than 1.3 million Rohingya remain displaced across South and Southeast Asia, including 1.2 million in sprawling refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh, according to the UN. Conflict, shrinking humanitarian aid and dangerous sea crossings continue to leave many members of the community displaced and vulnerable.

Hepsiburada ’nın 2017 yılında hayata geçirdiği Girişimci Kadınlara Teknoloji Gücü programı, kadınların e-ticarette işlerini kurmalarına ve büyütmelerine destek olmayı sürdürüyor.
Komisyon indirimleri, kadın kooperatiflerine süresiz kargo desteği, reklam avantajları, ürün fotoğrafçılığı, eğitim ve mentörlük gibi pek çok destek sunan program sayesinde bugüne kadar 8 binden fazla kadın kendi markasını kurdu. Bugün Hepsiburada’daki iş ortaklarının yüzde 25’ini girişimci kadınlar oluştururken, girişimci kadınların ve kadın kooperatiflerinin platformda satışa sunduğu ürün sayısı 134 milyonu aştı. Platformdaki girişimci kadınların cirosu yılın ilk dokuz ayında geçen yıla kıyasla yüzde 42, sipariş adedi ise yüzde 23 arttı.
Hepsiburada Kurumsal İletişim ve Sosyal Etki Grup Direktörü Canan Binal Yılmaz, programın dokuz yıllık yolculuğuna ilişkin şunları söyledi:
“2017 yılında, bu topraklarda doğan kadın markalarını Türkiye’de ve dünyada büyütmek hedefiyle yola çıktık. Dokuz yıldır kadınların e-ticarete girişte karşılaştıkları engelleri kaldırmak için çalışıyoruz. Ancak bizim için asıl başarı, kadınların e-ticarete adım atmaları kadar bu alanda kalıcı olmaları, rekabet güçlerini artırmaları ve markalarını büyütmeleri. Bu nedenle programımızı yalnızca ticari avantajlar sunan bir destek modeli olarak değil, eğitimden mentorluğa, yeni pazarlara erişimden marka görünürlüğüne uzanan bütüncül bir yapı olarak geliştiriyoruz. Kurumlar arası iş birliklerimiz, kadınların başarılarını yurt dışına taşıyan çalışmalarımız, Anadolu’nun farklı illerindeki buluşmalarımızla girişimci kadınların dijital ekonominin güçlü ve sürdürülebilir aktörleri olmalarını hedefliyoruz.”
Hepsiburada, girişimci kadınların ve kadın kooperatiflerinin e-ticarette sürdürülebilir büyümesini desteklemek amacıyla ticari avantajlardan eğitim ve pazarlama çözümlerine uzanan kapsamlı destekler sunuyor. Girişimci kadınlara yüzde 50 komisyon indirimi, 200 ürüne kadar profesyonel fotoğraf çekimi ve sponsorlu ürün reklamlarında kullanılmak üzere 5.000 TL HepsiAd reklam bakiyesi sağlanıyor. Ayrıca ön muhasebe, e-fatura ve stok takibi gibi iş süreçlerinde indirimli çözümler sunuluyor.
Kadın kooperatifleri ise ilk altı ay sıfır komisyon, sonrasında süresiz yüzde 1 komisyon avantajından yararlanıyor. İadeler dahil kargo giderleri karşılanırken 500 ürüne kadar profesyonel stüdyo çekimi desteği veriliyor. Hepsiburada, ücretsiz eğitimler ve platform içi görünürlük imkânlarıyla da girişimci kadınların ve kadın kooperatiflerinin daha fazla müşteriye ulaşmalarını ve işlerini büyütmelerini desteklemeyi sürdürüyor.

Türkiye'nin ev sahipliğinde Antalya'da düzenlenen COP31 kapsamında Sabancı Üniversitesi tarafından İstanbul Politikalar Merkezi (İPM) İklim Değişikliği Çalışmaları Koordinatörü Ümit Şahin moderatörlüğünde "İklim Müzakerelerinde Durum Değerlendirmesi: Fosil Yakıtlar, Adil Geçiş ve Öne Çıkan Öncelikler" başlıklı basın toplantısı gerçekleştirildi.
Toplantıda, COP31 müzakerelerinde gelinen son aşamayı değerlendiren Londra merkezli düşünce kuruluşu E3G Kıdemli Analisti Öykü Şenlen, zirve sona yaklaşırken tüm gözlerin sonuç karar metnine çevrildiğini belirtti.
Hafta başında yayımlanan taslak metinde, her ülkenin talep ettiği konuların yer aldığını ve ülkelerin çoğunun metin üzerinde çalışmaya hazır olduğunu COP31 Başkanlığına ilettiğini kaydeden Şenlen, müzakere salonlarının dışında da "gerçek bir ivmenin" söz konusu olduğunu dile getirdi.
Şenlen, Türkiye'nin COP31 Başkanlığı kapsamında açıkladığı küresel elektrifikasyon oranını 2035'e kadar yüzde 35'e çıkarma hedefine ülkelerin desteğinin arttığını belirterek, şunları kaydetti:
"Bu olumlu bir işaret ve daha fazla ülkenin katılmasını istiyoruz. Ancak bu ivmenin sonuç karar metnine de yansıdığını görmemiz gerekiyor. İlk taslakta elektrifikasyona yer verilmesi çok iyi bir gelişme ama elektrifikasyonun nasıl gerçekleştirileceği ve bu konudaki uzlaşmanın nasıl ilerleyeceği de önemli. Elektrifikasyona yenilenebilir enerji kaynakları öncülük etmeli, şebekeler ve enerji depolama sistemleri bunu desteklemeli. Ayrıca bu süreç, gelişmekte olan ülkeler açısından adil ve gerçekleştirilebilir olmalı."
Fosil yakıtlardan uzaklaşılması ve iklim finansmanına ilişkin kararların da karar metninde olması gerektiğinin altını çizen Şenlen, "İnsanlar iklim değişikliğinin etkilerini şimdiden yaşıyor ve ihtiyaç duyulan kaynaklarla mevcut kaynaklar arasındaki fark giderek büyüyor." dedi.
Şenlen, küresel sıcaklık artışının 1,5 dereceyi aşmasına ilişkin ifadelerin de COP31 karar metninde geri planda kalmaması gerektiğini belirterek, şöyle konuştu:
"Artık dünyanın en azından bir süreliğine 1,5 derece artış eşiğini aşmasının muhtemel olduğunu biliyoruz. Metin bu gerçeğe yanıt vermeli ve dünyanın 1,5 derece hedefini korumaya, mümkün olan en kısa sürede sıcaklık aşımını bu seviyeye geri döndürmeye hala bağlı olduğu yönünde siyasi bir mesaj vermeli."
Tufts Üniversitesi Fletcher Okulu Kıdemli Araştırmacısı Jennifer Morgan da COP31 kapsamında Danimarka, Almanya, İspanya ve Portekiz başta olmak üzere fosil yakıtlardan uzaklaşmaya yönelik yol haritasını açıklayan ülkelerin sayısının arttığını, bu konunun bir zamanlar "tabu" olduğunu ancak artık bunun yıkıldığını dile getirdi.
Bu ülkelerin fosil yakıtlardan uzaklaşma taahhütlerinin COP31'in sonuç metninde yer alma çağrısında bulunduğunu kaydeden Morgan, COP31 Başkanı Türkiye ve Müzakereler Başkanı Avustralya'nın bu çağrılara karşılık verecekleri yönünde büyük beklentiler olduğunu ifade etti.
Morgan, Türkiye ve Avustralya'nın da fosil yakıtlardan uzaklaşma konusunda çaba göstermesi gerektiğini belirterek, "Avustralya ise özellikle fosil yakıt ihracatını, komşularının kullanabileceği çok sayıda yeşil ürüne yönelik ihracatla değiştirmeli." dedi.
İPM İklim Değişikliği Çalışmaları Koordinatörü Şahin, Türkiye'nin bu ay başında açıkladığı 2040 Enerji Vizyonu'na atıfta bulunarak, bu planda 15 yıl içinde Türkiye'de petrol ve gaz tüketiminin kademeli olarak azalacağının öngörüldüğüne işaret etti.
Bunun da fosil yakıtlardan uzaklaşma sürecinin bir parçası olduğunu dile getiren Şahin, "Türkiye de bu kapsamdaki niyetini en azından bir fosil yakıtlardan uzaklaşma yol haritasına dönüştürebilir." dedi.
İPM İklim Değişikliği Araştırmacısı Onur Akgül, COP31 müzakereleri sona yaklaşırken "adil dönüşüm mekanizmasının" kurulmasına ilişkin somut bir ilerleme sağlanmadığının altını çizdi.
Türkiye'nin henüz kömürden çıkışa yönelik bir plan duyurmadığını kaydeden Akgül, Türkiye'nin "ülkenin makroekonomik önemini zedelemeden" 2036'ya kadar kömürden çıkışı sağlayabileceğini ifade etti.
İklim Ağı üyesi WWF Türkiye İklim ve Enerji Programı Kıdemli Uzmanı Pınar Gayretli de COP31 karar metninde fosil yakıtlardan uzaklaşma çağrısının yer alması gerektiğini dile getirerek, Türkiye'nin bu kapsamda liderlik yapabileceğini söyledi.
Uluslararası Kriyosfer İklim Girişimi Direktörü Pam Pearson ise küresel sıcaklık artışının 1,5 dereceyi aşmasının "neredeyse normalleştirildiğine" işaret ederek, "Bu aşımın kaçınılmaz olduğu ifade ediliyor ve bu geleceğe ait bir tehdit değil. Kriyosferde geri dönüşü olmayan eşikler her gün aşılıyor ve bu durum geçen yüzyılın ortalarından bu yana devam ediyor. Bu, umudumuzu yitirmemiz gerektiği anlamına gelmiyor. Aksine, emisyonları şimdi azaltmak için çok daha acil harekete geçmemiz gerektiği anlamına geliyor." diye konuştu.
Bilimsel verileri dikkate almak yerine müzakerelerde bunların sorgulanmasının "sorumsuzca ve tehlikeli" bir tutum olduğunu belirten Pearson, müzakerelerin her zaman küresel bilimsel araştırmaların bulgularını takip etmesinin büyük önem taşıdığını sözlerine ekledi.

The three presidents stood together for the official group shot ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum’s opening session. The high-level assembly drew leaders from across the Pacific, featuring Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Canada’s Mark Carney, Australia’s Anthony Albanese and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.
Taking the podium, Xi Jinping made a plea for closer Asia-Pacific ties in an era of sweeping global upheaval and rapid technological breakthroughs. He challenged member nations to prioritise innovation, openness and deeper integration, framing the goal as a shared regional community rooted in solidarity and inclusive development.
All eyes, however, were fixed on Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, who are slated to join Xi for separate trilateral talks . The rare sight of the Chinese, American and Russian presidents sharing a stage at the opening ceremony threw into sharp relief the diplomatic significance of the Shenzhen meeting .

With a broad smile and a firm handshake, US President Donald Trump greeted Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday 19 November 2026 , just hours before joining Chinese President Xi Jinping for trilateral talks. Walking into a compact meeting room at Kylin Villa, Trump pointed towards Putin beside the Russian flag and joked, "Who is he?" before adding: "He's my friend." A smiling Putin stepped forward to clasp his hand, exchanging a quiet word after Trump said, "Nice to see you."
Speaking in front of the television cameras, Trump insisted the pair had shared a "great relationship for many years" and said he hoped "a lot of wonderful things" would emerge from the session.
The 40-minute encounter , taking place on the fringes of the APEC summit, offered a fresh display of Trump’s personal affinity for Putin even as Russia’s war in Ukraine grinds on. Their last face-to-face meeting, in Alaska in 2025 , failed to produce a breakthrough to end the war, which has killed civilians and uprooted millions since the full-scale invasion in February 2022 .
Trump’s friendly overtures jarred with ongoing tensions between Moscow and Western governments over Ukraine. The bilateral sit-down led directly into a trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping , convening the American, Russian and Chinese presidents for closely watched diplomacy.

The International Court of Justice has upheld large parts of a genocide case against Myanmar linked to the 2017 conflict with its Rohingya minority. It called for it to pay reparations and let refugees return safely.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday found Myanmar in breach of several of its obligations under international treaties to prevent and not to commit genocide .
The ICJ's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said that the panel of 15 judges had decided by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya in Rakhine state .
The judges also found the country guilty of a series of other more specific violations by majority rulings.
"On the basis of all the evidence taken together, the Court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of... the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said.
Iwasawa said that Myanmar should make efforts to pay reparations to victims or their associates where possible and appropriate.
He also called for it to facilitate the safe return of refugees, and to take measures to investigate and if necessary prosecute individual wrongdoing by its nationals and security forces.
The ICJ said that by its consideration, the Rohingya constituted a distinct ethnic group with their own defining language and culture, as well as self-identifying as such. This means they qualified as a protected group for the purposes of international laws against genocide.
Myanmar's security forces "killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated acts of sexual violence, as well as extreme violence against children," and also attacked Rohingya as they tried to flee the fighting, the ICJ's Iwasawa said.
"The court is fully convinced that the 2017 clearance operations caused serious bodily and mental harm to a significant number of the protected group," Judge Iwasawa said.
Iwasawa also said that some civilian participation in the clearance operations could not necessarily be considered state-ordered or state-sanctioned behavior. But the court found that the government and security forces also made no meaningful efforts to prevent non-Rohingya civilian atrocities and if anything fanned the flames of ethnic and religious tension.
At one point reading the details of the findings, Iwasawa noted "Myanmar's failure, genuinely to investigate the alleged atrocities, and its refusal to facilitate access to evidence and witnesses, or provide information requested."
He said this meant it was possible the court did not have reliable knowledge of information available only from within Myanmar to which it was not given access.
There was no immediate response from the government in Myanmar or the military that's seen as the real underlying power.
Rohingya activist Yasmin Ullah — a Canadian citizen since 2016 but who was born in Rakhine state and who was a member of Gambia's delegation that filed the ICJ case — called the verdict more important for the world than for her community.
"The Rohingya never needed a court to tell us what happened to us," she said. "We needed the world to hear it, and today it has."
Wai Wai Nu, a Rohingya activist who directs the Women's Peace Network NGO, said the world's highest court's finding followed "decades" when "the Burmese military tried to erase our identity, deny our existence and dismiss our suffering."
And the co-chair of the Arakan Rohingya National Council, Nay San Lwin, said that for Ronihgya, "justice means the restoration of our citizenship, recognition of our identity and our safe and dignified return home."
Myanmar's shadow national unity government, which includes remnants of former President Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy Party, said it "respects the authority" of the ICJ.
It said that since the beginning of the "revolution against military dictatorship" in 2021, it had affirmed its "commitment to the rule of law, human rights, justice and states' obligations to prevent and punish genocide."
Myanmar was under nominally civilian rule at the time of the atrocities but the extent to which President Aung San Suu Kyi's government held sway over the military and its actions is debatable.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres welcomed Thursday's verdict, calling it a "powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide" and noting it was the first verdict of its kind against a state.
"Myanmar must act in accordance with its obligation to comply with the Court's decision," Guterres said in a statement, adding that this includes "the safe, voluntary and dignified return [of Rohingya] to their place of residence nad reunification of families."
Gambia's Justice Minister Dawda Jallow, who attended the hearing, spoke to reporters afterwards at the Peace Palace in The Hague.
"The victory belongs to the Rohingya," Jallow said. "They survived. They testified. And today, they will believe."
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband issued a statement saying the former colonial power was "taking immediate action today in light of this judgment."
Miliband said Britain would expel Myanmar's defense attache in London and was calling for a special UN Security Council session in response. He called on Myanmar to "comply fully with the judgment," and on the international community to "play its part in supporting implementation, accountability, and justice for the Rohingya."
UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the ruling "clearly concludes the State of Myanmar stands responsible for one of the most egregious crimes known to humankind."
The case centers around the military crackdown in Rakhine state on the country's western coastline against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017.
Violence had been brewing for several years beforehand, but the most intense phase of the military crackdown in the north of region was triggered by a coordinated attack by a Muslim militia group against several police and military installations and personnel in August 2017.
A UN fact finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the military clearance operations that followed. Around 700,000 people fled to Bangladesh, where most still reside in the world's largest refugee camp .
Gambia filed the complaint at The Hague in 2019, alleging a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder designed to wipe out the Rohingya minority in whole or in part.
Myanmar's influential military, now back in full de facto control of the country albeit amid a long-running civil war, has maintained that it was engaged in a legitimate counterinsurgency.
Aung San Suu Kyi , who was the civilian president at the time, took a slightly more nuanced stance, but nevertheless traveled to The Hague to contest the charges, calling them "incomplete and incorrect."
The case is likely to draw close attention from those pursuing ICJ prosecutions against Israel and Benjamin Netanyahu for the war in Gaza and against Russia and Vladimir Putin for the invasion of Ukraine.
